DevelopingUpdated 11:35 a.m. ET Wednesday

Putin agrees “in principle” to resume U.S.–Ukraine–Russia peace talks after Nov. 10, Kremlin says, as Russia frees an American

Latest CBS News · Wed 11:15 a.m.First reported by PBS NewsHour (The Associated Press) · Wed 9:15 a.m.

After about three hours with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg, Vladimir Putin agreed “in principle” to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kyiv after Nov. 10, his foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said, focused on “building a security system for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends” (The Associated Press via CTV News). Ushakov also said the proposals Witkoff brought “contained little that was useful,” and the Kremlin says any progress needs Ukraine to make “necessary decisions” (CBS News). Russia freed American Stephen Hubbard, jailed for more than four years; Witkoff’s praise of Putin as a “humanitarian” drew rebukes from Republican senators (CBS News).

  • Nov. 10 after which Putin agreed “in principle” to resume trilateral talks, Ushakov says (The Associated Press via CTV News)
  • 3 hours Witkoff and Putin talked at Constantine Palace; Jared Kushner joined by video link (The Associated Press via CTV News)
  • 4+ years Stephen Hubbard was jailed in Russia before his release Wednesday (CBS News)
  • 3 rounds of trilateral talks held early this year, in Abu Dhabi and Geneva, with little progress beyond prisoner exchanges (The Associated Press via CTV News)
  • 5 people killed and 25 wounded in overnight Russian attacks, Ukraine says (The Associated Press via CTV News)
  • Where and when the talks will happen, and whether Zelenskyy will take part; he says only a leaders’ summit can break the impasse (The Associated Press via CTV News)
  • Whether a Trump–Putin–Xi meeting, which Russian officials call “possible,” goes ahead; Ukrainian officials have balked at it (CBS News)

What we know

  • Putin agreed “in principle” to resume trilateral talks after Nov. 10, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov said after the St. Petersburg meeting (The Associated Press via CTV News).
  • Russia released American Stephen Hubbard; Trump says no swap was needed (CBS News).
  • Zelenskyy told Fox News that freezing the conflict is the “minimum” needed to end the war (The Associated Press via CTV News).

Not yet known

  • A date and place for the talks, and who will sit at the table.
  • What was in the proposals Witkoff brought, which the Kremlin attributes to Ukraine and the EU (CBS News).
Confirmation tracker 9 outlets

Verified: the Kremlin’s own adviser announced the talks, reported by The Associated Press, CBS News, PBS NewsHour, BBC News, Kyiv Independent and CBC News.

How this story developed

  1. Wed 11:15 a.m.Ushakov says the proposals Witkoff brought, which he attributes to Ukraine and the EU, “contained little that was useful”; Russian officials tell Witkoff a Trump–Putin–Xi meeting is “possible.” (CBS News)
  2. Wed 10:57 a.m.Republican senators Thom Tillis and John Cornyn rebuke Witkoff for calling Putin a “humanitarian” after Hubbard’s release. (CBS News)
  3. Wed 10:26 a.m.Putin agrees “in principle” to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kyiv after Nov. 10, Ushakov says after the three-hour meeting. (The Associated Press via CTV News)
  4. Wed 9:15 a.m.Russia frees American Stephen Hubbard, imprisoned for more than four years, during Witkoff’s visit. (PBS NewsHour)
CanadaVoting today

Albertans vote today on a path to leaving Canada

Polls are open 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. MT (11 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET) on 10 questions, with some open later. Question 10 asks whether Alberta stays in Canada or starts the legal steps toward a later, binding vote on leaving. More than 1.35 million people, about 43% of eligible voters, voted early or by mail. Ballots are counted by hand, Question 10 first. More than 100 polling stations opened late, so some stay open past 8 p.m. MT, the latest until 10 p.m. MT (midnight ET) at Edmonton’s Westminster School, and Elections Alberta says no results will be released until every poll has closed (CBC News). Results on Question 10 are expected between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. MT Tuesday, Elections Alberta says (CTV News).

    Smaller newsrooms

    Today’s top five from independent and northern newsrooms, with an eye on the Arctic. Updated Monday morning.

    1. Nunatsiaq NewsNunavut Arctic

      Nunavut teachers feeling the strain as student support workers disappear

      Federal Inuit Child First money no longer covers most school requests, so classrooms have fewer support assistants this year and teachers report burnout. Ottawa has extended the program a year with a $115-million top-up and now reviews school requests case by case.

      By Miriam Lafontaine
    2. Yellowknifer (NNSL)Nunavut Arctic

      Coast Guard’s only large drone put through Arctic trials in Iqaluit

      The Canadian Coast Guard is testing its lone Hermes 900 surveillance drone out of Iqaluit until spring 2027, for jobs like tracking ships, spotting pollution and scouting ice.

      By William Koblensky Varela, Local Journalism Initiative
    3. Nunatsiaq NewsNunavut Arctic

      Qikiqtarjuaq man loses his jury trial after sleeping through its start

      About 60 prospective jurors turned out in September. A judge ruled oversleeping was no excuse, so the sexual assault trial resumes before a judge alone in February.

      By Miriam Lafontaine
    4. The TyeeBritish Columbia

      Incumbent mayors swept out across B.C., Kamloops included

      Kamloops Mayor Reid Hamer-Jackson finished fourth, and sitting mayors also lost in Surrey, Langley, West Vancouver, Quesnel and Penticton.

      By Tyler Olsen
    5. Yukon NewsYukon Arctic

      Yukon’s mid-year budget update shows restraint, for now

      Columnist Keith Halliday says the supplementary budget trims the deficit slightly and keeps public-service staffing nearly flat, but a costly union contract and shaky bond markets could undo it.

      By Keith Halliday

    Canada and the U.S.

    Where the trade war stands, what changed this week, and what comes next. Every line links to the newsroom that reported it. Updated Wednesday, Oct. 21, 11:22 a.m. ET.

    Trade talksSuspended since Aug. 22No talks are under way. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has said Canada is likely to come back to the table after the Quebec and Alberta votes (Inside U.S. Trade). Carney says Canada will return “when the Americans are ready” (CNBC). Canadian officials have told industry groups they do not expect a deal before the Nov. 3 U.S. midterms, three sources told CBC News.
    50%U.S. tariff on about US$20 billion of Canadian goods, including dairy, alcohol, cement and hockey gear. In force since Aug. 22.NPR · The Hill
    15–50%Canada’s counter-tariffs on nearly $20 billion of U.S. goods, more than 700 products, from steel to appliances. In force since Sept. 8.Al Jazeera · CNBC
    ~35%Total U.S. duty on Canadian softwood lumber after the Commerce Department’s latest review, the BC Lumber Trade Council says. Set Oct. 14.CTV News · CBC News
    AnnualCUSMA review. The U.S. declined on July 1 to extend the trade deal for 16 years, so it now faces a review every year.CBC News · National Observer

    How U.S. media see Canada

    American coverage this week reads Alberta’s vote through Trump’s trade war and his “51st state” talk, and through oil: about 90% of Alberta’s crude exports go to the U.S. (AP). CNN’s post-vote report keeps the U.S. in the frame, noting separatists’ meetings with U.S. officials in Washington (CNN). After the vote, AP framed Alberta’s rejection of separation as a win for Carney won under the shadow of Trump’s annexation threats (AP); the progressive magazine Mother Jones called it a no to a “MAGA-aligned” campaign (Mother Jones), while the conservative site Breitbart also called it a win for Carney and noted separatists’ view that Trump’s tariffs and mockery helped the No side (Breitbart); on voting day, Fox News noted Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had called Alberta “a natural partner for the U.S.” (Fox News). On trade, U.S. outlets reported a food importer’s lawsuit challenging the legal basis of Trump’s 50% tariffs on Canadian goods (Newsweek, Quartz, Fox Business), and WAMC public radio aired a Canadian senator saying the relationship with the U.S. has changed for good (WAMC). Here is what American newsrooms are telling their readers about Canada, newest first.

    • Fox BusinessBusiness newsWed Oct. 21US food importer sues Trump administration over 50% tariffs on Canadian goodsMichael Sinkewicz, at the business network, leads with the cost to a family-run New Jersey importer, about $40 million a year on Canadian cheese, and sets the suit among other court challenges to Trump’s tariffs. It gives the administration’s case that the tariffs answer “discriminatory” Canadian trade practices, and both Ottawa’s and Washington’s accounts of why talks broke down.
    • NewsweekMagazineWed Oct. 21Trump Accused of Unlawfully Invoking 1930s Law for Canada TariffsFaye James frames the Gellert Global Group suit as a legal test of the administration’s use of Section 338 for the 50% tariffs on Canadian cheese and other goods, laying out the importer’s argument that later trade laws supersede it, and noting the White House says it will vigorously defend the tariffs.
    • WAMCPublic radioTue Oct. 20Canadian lawmaker: Relationship with U.S. has completely changedThe upstate New York public broadcaster’s Pat Bradley gives the floor to independent Canadian Senator Martine Hébert, speaking at SUNY Plattsburgh, who says the tariffs are “going to lead to permanent changes” and that Canada is diversifying its trade.
    • Mother JonesMagazineTue Oct. 20Alberta Says No to MAGA-Aligned Independence CampaignSatchel Walton, at the progressive magazine, casts the result as a setback for a right-wing, MAGA-linked separatist movement and ties the vote to Trump’s “51st state” threats and tariffs, while noting Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa predate Trump.
    • TimeMagazineTue Oct. 20Alberta Voted to Stay in Canada. That Doesn’t Quite Settle the Separatist DebateChantelle Lee argues the grievances behind the movement, over federal energy policy and representation, remain unresolved, and sets the vote against the trade war and Trump’s Oct. 14 “51st state” remark. It quotes political scientist Jared Wesley: “Albertans are overwhelmingly opposed to Trump’s trade war and even more averse to becoming the 51st state.”
    • BreitbartNews siteTue Oct. 20Alberta Secession Referendum FailsJohn Hayward, at the conservative site, calls the result a win for Carney and Canadian unity and keeps Trump in the frame: his Kansas rally offer to let Canada keep hockey and “O Canada” as a state anthem, separatists’ view that his tariffs and mockery helped the No side, and NDP Leader Avi Lewis’s call for an investigation into alleged U.S. support for the referendum.
    • CNNTV networkTue Oct. 20Alberta rejects secession referendum, chooses to remain part of Canada, CBC projectsMax Saltman lays out separatists’ grievances over representation, climate policy and the “lucrative fossil fuel industry,” and the U.S. angle: separatists met U.S. officials in Washington, and one separatist lawyer said the Trump administration would be the one “to have the guts” to recognize an independent Alberta.
    • The Associated PressNews agencyTue Oct. 20Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unityRob Gillies calls the result a win for Carney and for Canadian unity, won while Trump’s trade war and “51st state” threats hung over the country, and says those threats helped Carney gain support in Alberta. It also notes separatist leaders vow their movement will persist. Carried by NPR, CBS News, the conservative-leaning Washington Times and the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin.

    This week

    1. Tue Oct. 20

      No trade deal expected before the U.S. midterms, sources say. Canadian officials have spent recent weeks telling industry groups they do not expect an agreement with the U.S. before the Nov. 3 elections, CBC News reports, citing three sources. Officials on both sides remain in contact, but there is no substantive negotiation, the report says.

      CBC News · Newsquawk
    2. Tue Oct. 20

      Budget watchdog cuts growth forecast: “Additional trade measures and ongoing uncertainty are weighing on growth.” The Parliamentary Budget Officer now expects Canada’s economy to grow 0.9% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027, down from 1.1% and 1.6% in June, after the new U.S. tariffs and Canada’s counter-tariffs.

      BNN Bloomberg (Canadian Press) · CTV News · CBC News
    3. Tue Oct. 20

      U.S. food importer sues to block the 50% tariffs: “No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf.” Gellert Global Group, with the Liberty Justice Center, filed in the U.S. Court of International Trade on behalf of itself and a proposed class of importers, arguing Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act, never before used for tariffs, does not cover the Canadian policies Trump cited. The suit also seeks refunds of duties on Canadian cheese collected before a 30-day waiting period ended, the group says.

      Global News (Canadian Press) · Bloomberg (subscribers) · CNBC · The Associated Press · Quartz · Liberty Justice Center
    4. Tue Oct. 20

      U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra: “We’re not in a trade war.” In a CTV News video posted Tuesday, Hoekstra rejected the view that the Canada–U.S. relationship has ruptured.

      CTV News (video)
    5. Tue Oct. 20

      Alberta votes to stay in Canada, CBC News projects. Carney: Albertans “chose unity.” With 1,316,313 votes counted on the separation question as of 1 a.m. MT, 1,005,641 were for remaining in Canada and 310,672 for a binding separation referendum, Global News reports; results on the other nine questions are expected by Wednesday. AP put the split at about 76% to 23%. Premier Danielle Smith said Tuesday night: “I will honour this mandate from Albertans and will not be holding another referendum on this issue.” U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has said he expects Canada to come back to trade talks after the Alberta and Quebec votes.

      CBC News · Global News · Global News (Smith) · BNN Bloomberg (CTV News) · CTV News · The Associated Press · Inside U.S. Trade · Prime Minister’s Office · CP24
    6. Mon Oct. 19

      Trump softens on Bombardier: “we’re not hurting them if they’re in Kansas.” In Wichita, he said of the Canadian jet maker’s U.S. workers, “we’ll take care of those people and the jobs,” Reuters reports. He threatened in September to bar Bombardier from the U.S. market; it has about 3,500 U.S. employees, over 40% of them in Wichita, and its shares rose 2.1% on Tuesday. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc responded Tuesday, stressing the importance of protecting the aerospace sector, CTV News reports.

      CTV News (Reuters) · CBC News · Bloomberg (subscribers) · CTV News (video)
    7. Mon Oct. 19

      Bank of Canada: “renewed trade tensions are dampening firms’ sentiment.” Its third-quarter Business Outlook Survey says most responses came in before the Canada–U.S. talks broke down, and that the new tariffs and counter-tariffs are putting upward pressure on costs, prices and inflation expectations.

      Bank of Canada · Castanet (Canadian Press)
    8. Mon Oct. 19

      Cleveland-Cliffs CEO: “Stelco can immediately bring back all the temporarily laid-off workers” if Ottawa curbs galvanized steel imports. On a call about third-quarter results, in which Stelco had its strongest quarter since the 2024 takeover, Lourenco Goncalves called Canada’s galvanized market “clearly oversupplied.” Stelco is idling its galvanizing lines indefinitely; he said about 2,000 Canadian jobs are preserved.

      BNN Bloomberg (Canadian Press) · CHCH News · Manufacturing Dive
    9. Fri Oct. 16

      Ottawa threatens forced sale of Stelco’s assets: “they must keep the jobs in Canada.” Industry Minister Mélanie Joly warned U.S. owner Cleveland-Cliffs, which has cited U.S. tariffs in cutting up to 500 Hamilton jobs, that it could be made to sell under the Investment Canada Act. CEO Lourenco Goncalves called it “bullying and harassment.”

      CTV News · BNN Bloomberg
    10. Thu Oct. 15

      Carney: “Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.” At a Calgary rally before Alberta’s vote, the prime minister urged Albertans to stay. He did not name the U.S. in that line.

      The Associated Press · Time · PBS NewsHour

    What comes next

    1. Wed Oct. 21, 2 p.m.

      Carney and Ford announce support for industries hit by U.S. tariffs. The prime minister and Ontario Premier Doug Ford meet on Parliament Hill, with a joint announcement on support for the steel and auto sectors to follow, The Canadian Press reports; support for critical minerals is also under consideration, a source says. The package includes funding for automakers making clean investments, a source tells CBC News.

      CBC News · CTV News (Canadian Press) · Prime Minister’s itinerary
    2. Tue Nov. 3

      U.S. midterms. Maine and Michigan, both tied closely to Canada, have competitive races. Sen. Susan Collins has distanced herself from the tariffs, and Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has called for the dispute to end. Canadian officials do not expect a trade deal before the vote, CBC News reports.

      CBC News · Atlantic Council · Inside U.S. Trade
    3. Thu Nov. 5

      Federal budget, two days after the U.S. midterms. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced the date in question period on Tuesday, with U.S. tariffs and Canada’s counter-tariffs still in force.

      Global News · CBC News
    4. Watching

      Oil and autos. Oil has been spared so far. The average tariff on Canadian autos and parts rose from 0.2% in February 2025 to 9.2% this August.

      Atlantic Council

      About Palindrome

      How we work, where our news comes from, and how to reach us.

      Methodology

      A story gets a full Palindrome summary only when six independent newsrooms have reported it. Outlets with the same owner count as one.

      Until then it runs as developing news, with a meter showing how many outlets have it. Breaking news can run sooner, credited to the outlet that reported it, and is labelled unconfirmed.

      Every summary links to the reporting it draws on. Tapping a story takes you to the newest, fullest report, and each story credits the outlet that reported it first: the earliest report we found.
